chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Ben Webster permuting chords
summary: Ben ran every chord permutation; Maxwell says these players turned theory into reality.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. But Ben would stand in a corner of the room and run changes, you know. He'd run arpeggios and I guess a lot like I've read about Col. trane used to do, off the bridge or something.* He would just permute the chords, you know, like you'd take a four- part chord, there's 12 ways you can play it, four times three times two. And he would take it from every angle and go through all his chords. God, what tedious work.

I mean, some of these guys, conservatory musicians talk about jazz players, they ought to practice one-half as hard and one-half as intelligently or as musically as these guys. Because these guys were not only practicing the technique of their instruments, like Ben would permute, you know, but he was practicing instant composition at the same time, you know. Theory, in the hands of guys like Ben Webster, and you told me about Dizzy, I know Dizzy really knows what he's doing, theory
*Sonny Rollins, not Coltrane, practiced on the walkway of the Williamsburgh Bridge during his voluntary retirement of 1959-1961.
was not the right word to use for them, because what they were doing wasn't theory, they made it reality, you know. They were doing it, it wasn't theory. They turned it into the real thing.
